terms.gloss: pull oneself together, recover one’s composure
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.78: quid est autem sē ipsum colligere, nisi dissipātās animī partēs rūrsum in suum locum cōgere? (Lewis & Short s.v. colligō)
Caes. BC 3.65: sē ex timōre (colligere; Lewis & Short)
Traupman p. 106: pull oneself together, sē colligere
terms.comment: “To gather oneself together”: Cicero explains it as bringing the scattered parts of the mind back into place. Lewis & Short calls it very frequent and classical; so also animum colligere.

evidence: Ter. Ad. 323–325: Quid festīnās, mī Geta? Animam recipe.
Liv. 2.50.10: ā pavōre animum (recipere; Lewis & Short s.v. recipiō)
terms.comment: Animam recipere is to get one’s breath back; animum recipere, in Livy, to recover from a fright.

sources: Lewis & Short: colligo · Lewis & Short: recipio
